steps.title: Turn clues into constraints
steps.content: A seating or ordering puzzle gives relationships that must all hold. Translate words such as before, after, immediately next to, left of and between into constraints before choosing an arrangement.
steps.example: If A is before B and B is before C, the order must be A–B–C.

steps.title: Apply an ordering clue
steps.prompt: A is before B. B is before C. Which order is possible?
steps.explanation: Both constraints are satisfied only by A before B before C.

steps.title: Use a table or slots
steps.content: For position puzzles, draw numbered slots. For assignment puzzles, make a grid with people on one axis and attributes on the other. Mark confirmed facts and eliminate impossible combinations.
steps.tip: Do not keep the whole puzzle in your head. Write every fixed constraint.

steps.title: Place the middle person
steps.prompt: Four people P, Q, R and S sit in a row. P is left of Q, R is right of Q, and S is left of P. Who is second from the left?
steps.explanation: The only order satisfying all clues is S–P–Q–R. P is second from the left.

steps.title: Check every clue
steps.content: A candidate arrangement is valid only if it satisfies every statement. If two arrangements remain possible, do not claim a conclusion that is true in only one of them.

questions.prompt: A is taller than B. B is taller than C. Who is shortest?
questions.explanation: A > B > C, so C is shortest.

questions.prompt: Four tasks W, X, Y, Z are ordered. W is before X, X before Y and Y before Z. Which is first?
In a row of five people, the middle position is:
questions.explanation: The third position is the middle of five positions.

questions.prompt: A is immediately left of B. Which pair order is fixed?
options: A and B must be at the ends
questions.explanation: Immediately left means A is directly before B in the row.

questions.prompt: If two arrangements satisfy all given clues, what can you conclude about an extra statement true in only one arrangement?
questions.explanation: A conclusion must hold in every valid arrangement; one counterexample is enough to show it is not guaranteed.
